summary.text: A finite calculation gives \(a(5)=171\), with \(19\mid171\), and \(a(6)\equiv3\pmod{18}\). Since \(2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}\), it follows that \(2^{a(6)}+1\equiv2^3+1=9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\), so the division defining the seventh term is not exact.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by showing that the first six terms are integers but that the proposed seventh term is not.

Let
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}.
\]
The first few applications of the recurrence give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=\frac{2^{a(2)}+1}{a(1)}=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,\\
a(4)&=\frac{2^{a(3)}+1}{a(2)}=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,\\
a(5)&=\frac{2^{a(4)}+1}{a(3)}=\frac{2^9+1}{3}
      =\frac{513}{3}=171.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the next term is
\[
a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
We will both verify that this quotient is an integer and determine its residue modulo \(18\). For that purpose, compute \(2^{171}\) modulo \(162=2\cdot81\).

First, modulo \(81\),
\[
2^9=512\equiv 26\pmod{81}.
\]
Squaring gives
\[
2^{18}\equiv 26^2=676\equiv 28\pmod{81},
\]
and hence
\[
2^{27}=2^{18}2^9\equiv 28\cdot26=728\equiv-1\pmod{81}.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^{54}\equiv1\pmod{81}.
\]
Since \(171=3\cdot54+9\), we therefore have
\[
2^{171}=(2^{54})^3 2^9\equiv 26\pmod{81}.
\]
Both \(2^{171}\) and \(26\) are even. Consequently their difference is divisible by both \(81\) and \(2\); because \(81\) and \(2\) are coprime, the difference is divisible by \(162\). Thus
\[
2^{171}\equiv26\pmod{162},
\]
and so
\[
2^{171}+1\equiv27\pmod{162}.
\]
Equivalently, for some integer \(t\),
\[
2^{171}+1=162t+27=9(18t+3).
\]
This proves that division by \(9\) is exact and, more importantly, that
\[
a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}=18t+3\equiv3\pmod{18}.
\]
(The resulting integer is
\(332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761\), but its residue modulo \(18\) is all that is needed.)

Now consider the recurrence at \(n=7\). Since \(a(5)=171\), integrality of \(a(7)\) would require
\[
171\mid 2^{a(6)}+1.
\]
Because \(171=9\cdot19\), this would in particular imply
\[
19\mid 2^{a(6)}+1.
\]
We show that this necessary condition fails.

Modulo \(19\), one has
\[
2^9=512\equiv18\equiv-1\pmod{19},
\]
so
\[
2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}.
\]
We already proved that \(a(6)\equiv3\pmod{18}\), so write \(a(6)=18t+3\). Then
\[
2^{a(6)}=2^{18t+3}=(2^{18})^t2^3
   \equiv 1^t\cdot8
   \equiv8\pmod{19}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2^{a(6)}+1\equiv9\pmod{19}.
\]
Since \(9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\), the integer \(2^{a(6)}+1\) is not divisible by \(19\), and hence cannot be divisible by \(171\). Thus
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{171}
\]
is not an integer.

Accordingly, the recurrence already fails to produce an integer at its seventh term. Therefore the conjecture that every term of A078590 is an integer is false.
